computation.ES_vs_VaR_distinction: VaR = quantile at α (loss equaled/exceeded 2.5% of time). ES = average loss GIVEN that loss exceeds VaR (tail mean beyond threshold). ES > VaR for continuous distributions because it weights the extreme tail.

formula_basis: MAR33 parametric ES under normality: ES_α = σ × φ(z_α) / (1 - α), where φ(z) = (1/√2π)e^(-z²/2), z_α = Φ⁻¹(α)
weakest_point: Parametric ES assumes normal distribution. FRTB mandates historical simulation or GARCH-filtered historical simulation. The φ(z)/α formula is exact only under normality; real P&L is fat-tailed, making parametric ES underestimate true tail risk.

computation.ES_vs_VaR_distinction: ES_99% = 2.665 vs VaR_99% = 2.3263, ratio = 1.1456. ES is only 14.6% above VaR at 99%. At 97.5%, ES/VaR = 1.1927. The ratio grows as α decreases because tail density relative to tail probability increases.

formula_basis: MAR33 parametric ES under normality: ES_α = σ × φ(z_α) / (1 - α)
weakest_point: At 99%, ES/VaR ≈ 1.15 under normality. FRTB's 97.5% ES produces ES/VaR ≈ 1.19 — a tighter tail definition but higher multiplier relative to VaR. This asymmetry is key to FRTB's more conservative treatment of tail risk.

formula_basis: MAR33 FRTB: ES_LH = ES_10 × √(LH/10), where LH varies by risk factor (MAR33 Table: 10d for major FX, large-cap EQ; 20d for G10 IR; 40d for emerging FX, IG credit; 120d for certain commodities). Scaling assumes i.i.d. daily returns.
weakest_point: √(LH/10) scaling is a conservative approximation. It implicitly assumes returns are independent and identically distributed across the horizon. For discontinuous or path-dependent payoffs (e.g., structured products, exotic options), this scaling underestimates risk because it ignores jump risk and liquidity effects that scale nonlinearly with horizon.

computation.fractional_tail_problem: With 20 obs at 97.5%, the expected number of tail observations is exactly 0.5 — a fractional count with no natural integer interpretation
computation.convention_rationale: Banks typically round UP to ensure conservative VaR/ES. Alternative conventions include LINEAR INTERPOLATION (rank-based) or ROUND-TO-NEAREST, but these are less conservative.
computation.note_on_small_sample: 20 observations is far too small for reliable ES estimation. Basel/FTC guidelines recommend 250+ observations minimum (1 year) or 500+ (multi-year). With 20 obs, statistical error dominates.

formula_basis: MAR33 historical simulation ES: ES_α = (1/|T|) × Σ_{t∈T} |P&L_t|, where T = {t: P&L_t ≤ VaR_α}. The set T contains all observations whose loss equals or exceeds the α-quantile.
weakest_point: With only 20 observations, the 97.5% quantile falls at the fractional position 19.5/20. Using ceiling convention (1 observation) gives ES = -45. Using interpolation or floor would give different results. This discrete approximation error is severe with small samples — the difference between floor(0) and ceiling(1) observations doubles the ES from 0 to 45. Banks must use sufficient historical depth (≥250 days) per MAR33.
